subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Wireless Charging for EVs
description: Learn Wireless Charging for EVs in one minute.

hook.text: Imagine parking your car over a pad in the garage and it charges without plugging in anything.

buildup.text: Wireless charging uses magnetic resonance to transfer energy through the air between two coils.

discovery.text: One coil sits buried in the ground, the other under the car—energy transfers across the gap.

twist.text: Current wireless systems lose about 10 percent more energy than cables, making them less efficient.

climax.text: Some cities are testing wireless charging pads built into roads so cars could charge while driving.

punchline.text: Charging without a cable trades a little efficiency for total convenience.

quiz.question: How does wireless EV charging transfer energy?
options: Via magnetic resonance between two coils

details.summary: Wireless EV charging uses electromagnetic induction between coils embedded in the ground and the vehicle floor to transfer power without plugging in, promising effortless charging in parking spots.
details.whyItMatters: Wireless charging could eliminate the inconvenience of cables and connectors, making EV ownership as seamless as parking in a garage and finding the car charged every morning automatically.
takeaways: A transmitter coil in the ground induces current in a receiver on the car
Efficiency currently reaches 90 to 93 percent, close to wired charging
Dynamic wireless charging from roads could eventually charge cars while driving

faq.question: How efficient is wireless EV charging compared to plugging in?
faq.answer: Current wireless systems achieve about 90 to 93 percent efficiency, only slightly lower than wired charging. Improvements in coil design and alignment technology are closing this gap further.

faq.question: Is wireless charging while driving technically possible?
faq.answer: Yes. Several pilot projects in Sweden and South Korea have embedded charging coils under roads. The technology works but the infrastructure cost of electrifying highways remains a significant barrier to scale.
